newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels capture key town and press on. [CORRECTED 09:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels capture key town and press on. [CORRECTED 09:35 GMT]

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Wednesday his forces had captured the northeastern (corrects direction from northwestern) town of Isiro after heavy fighting and were moving towards Buta, 450 km (280 miles) east of Gbadolite, the jungle palace of Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), said Isiro fell late on Tuesday to a multi-pronged rebel advance against one of Africa's most notoriously ill-disciplined armies.
ADFL officials said the rebels had also assumed control of Isiro airstrip and consolidated positions outside the town.
Kabila said government troops and foreign mercenaries had retreated to Buta, the next stop on the road towards Mobutu's multi-million-dollar residence.

In the capital Kinshasa, a senior government defence official said the rebels had captured the town of Bafwasende in eastern Zaire and described Isiro as under serious threat. Kabila told Reuters his forces took Bafwasende on Sunday.
There was no independent confirmation of Isiro's fall although aid workers in Bukavu reported fighting on several fronts between the rebels and Zaire's ragged army.
Isiro, a connecting point to Uganda, Sudan and the Central African Republic, was a strategic base for the government's troops and mercenaries.

"Our forces are now in complete control of Isiro. The town was taken late on Tuesday," Kabila said. ADFL officials said Kabila's units were on Wednesday conducting mop-up operations in Isiro and had completely seized its airstrip.

Asked earlier on Wednesday about his reaction to a proposal by EU special envoy Aldo Ajello for a regional heads of state summit on the Zaire crisis, Kabila said any such meeting would be useless without the participation of himself and his group.
Kabila said no one had so far solicited his views on how to resolve the conflict in Africa's second largest country, yet his Alliance was the major player.

"We are part of the Zaire game, yet no one bothers to invite us to regional meetings on Zaire. We welcome any efforts towards resolving the Zaire problem but not inviting us to such a meeting does not and cannot solve the country's problems," he said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Kabila told 1,200 newly-trained troops that Mobutu was so panic-stricken by the lightning rebel advance that he now spent his nights in Bangui, capital of the Central African Republic, 275 km (180 miles) from Gbadolite.

"Our advance has caused a lot of panic in the government. The panic is so much that Mobutu now sleeps in Bangui and only comes to Gbadolite in the morning," Kabila told thousands of excited Bukavu residents who watched the rebels' parade.
"We intend to make life impossible for Mobutu. We will deal with him once and for all," he told chanting residents.
Kabila said up to 15,000 new rebels were training in Bukavu and urged parents to encourage their sons to join the rebels.
Kabila said government forces backed by warplanes and Russian-built MI-24 (Hind) helicopters had bombarded rebel positions around the town of Lubutu, a gateway to the city of Kisangani.
Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, is the main base for government forces seeking to reverse Kabila's stunning battlefield victories in the last four months.
Aid officials in Bukavu said some 1,200 Zaireans including 300 soldiers from the mining town of Kalemie had reached neighbouring Zambia's port town of Mpulungu via Lake Tanganyika late on Tuesday.

They said the Zaireans, many diseased and in bad shape, fled Kalemie after it fell to Kabila's forces almost two weeks ago. They spent a couple of days on the lake after their three barges ran out of fuel before Zambian authorities came to their rescue.
Kabila says he has seized a border strip about 1,400 km (875 miles) long since the revolt began in October.

In Kisangani, headquarters of the counter-offensive launched by the army on January 20, relief officials said more and more trapped Rwandan Hutu refugees were arriving near the village of Tingi Tingi 200 km (125 miles).
Brenda Barton, spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme in Kisangani, said thousands were arriving at Tingi Tingi from Amisi where the rebels captured a refugee camp and airstrip last week.
Tingi Tingi already hosts one camp of 120,000 refugees and the new arrivals were forming a second makeshift one of 35,000.
The Hutu refugees fled fearing reprisals following the 1994 genocide by hardline Hutus of minority Tutsis in Rwanda. Up to 700,000 refugees returned home to Rwanda in December.
